 Thanksgiving meal planning tips to reduce stress and improve food safety
 Early preparation can simplify holiday cooking
 Published 
 October 23, 2026 - 7:00 a.m. 
 AD 
 A month before Thanksgiving is the perfect time to start planning. With a little preparation now, you can enjoy the holiday with less stress and more time spent with family and friends. By spreading out shopping, food preparation and organizing tasks over the next few weeks, you'll be well on your way to a smooth and memorable Thanksgiving celebration.
 Thanksgiving is often considered the biggest meal of the year, and pulling it all together can feel overwhelming if everything is left until the last minute. Begin by thinking through your menu, shopping needs, refrigerator and freezer space, and cooking schedule. Ask yourself:
 AD 
 —Can some groceries be purchased ahead of time?
 —Which dishes can be prepared and frozen in advance?
 —Do you have enough refrigerator space for ingredients and leftovers?
 —Will your oven accommodate all the dishes that need to be cooked or reheated on Thanksgiving Day?
 Thanksgiving planning doesn't have to fall on one person's shoulders. Invite family members to help create the menu and prepare for the holiday. Assign age-appropriate tasks such as setting the table, preparing side dishes or helping with cleanup. When family members contribute to the planning process, they're often more excited to participate in making the meal a success.
 If guests offer to bring a dish, take them up on the offer. Appetizers, salads, breads, desserts and beverages are excellent choices that can help reduce your workload while adding variety to the meal.
 AD 
 As you prepare for Thanksgiving, don't forget food safety is just as important as menu planning. The Partnership for Food Safety Education's "The Story of Your Dinner" resource provides holiday meal-planning guidance along with recipes, food safety videos, fact sheets and activities for children. It's a useful tool for families looking to make food safety part of their holiday traditions. Learn more at www.fightbac.org/food-safety-education/the-story-of-your-dinner/.
 When it comes to preparing the turkey, handling leftovers and preventing foodborne illness, the USDA's Your Safe Thanksgiving Guide offers practical, science-based recommendations for safely selecting, thawing, cooking and serving poultry. Access the guide at www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/poultry/your-safe-thanksgiving-guide.
 Have a last-minute food safety question? The USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline is staffed by food safety specialists who can answer questions about safely handling meat, poultry and egg products. The hotline is available from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday and is even open on Thanksgiving Day from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Call the hotline at 1-888-674-6854 or email MPHotline@usda.gov.
 A stress-free Thanksgiving doesn't happen by accident. It starts with a plan, a little preparation and a willingness to share the workload. By shopping early, preparing make-ahead dishes, involving family and friends, and keeping food safety in mind, you'll be ready to focus on what matters most: enjoying good food and making memories with the people around your table.
 Kate Shumaker is an OSU Extension family and consumer sciences educator and may be called at 330-674-3015. Like and follow on Facebook @OSUEXTHolmes or visit holmes.osu.edu.
